name: Bilal Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we aren't selling anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My week is lectures for electronic engineering, a lot of lab sessions with soldering irons, and then Fridays I go to the mosque with a couple of friends from my corridor. At weekends I work in my family's showroom, Hansen Tile and Floor, on the edge of town, helping customers choose tiles and doing the invoices. I live in student housing, and I cook for myself mostly, so I've learned a lot of rice.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up in electronics?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I liked taking things apart when I was small. My dad is a tiler, and he'd let me wire the showroom lights. He wanted me to learn something that isn't kneeling on floors all day, and I wanted to understand what's inside the box. I use an AI tool sometimes when a circuit doesn't make sense, but I always rebuild it myself to check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, that seems reasonable. A lot of new things are overrated, and the useful bits stay. I'd tell my friends that we still have to learn properly, and I'd tell my dad that he doesn't need to change the showroom's ordering system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be calm. My degree stays valuable, and my family's business keeps going. I've got a future that I can see, which is to graduate, work for a few years, and then maybe start something of my own, with Dad's advice. Nothing in that picture shakes me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. Keep studying, keep the weekend shifts at the showroom, and do one small project a term, maybe a lighting controller for the shop. I'd apply for a summer job at an electronics firm. And I'd keep using AI sometimes, but only to understand, not to copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, I'd say. A normal level of exam stress and nothing more. My family's finances are fine, though we're careful, because Dad's business goes up and down with the building trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the family firm goes up and down. How do the quiet months affect your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad's business is the thing I watch. When builders slow down, he has a quiet month. We've had two bad winters, and Mum cuts back on everything. But that's cycles, and it's what you expect with a small firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your small project be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't see much to change in this world. If I'm honest, it makes me more patient. I can spend the next few years building a skill without worrying that the ground will move.

say: I'd say it's **reasonable**: new things are overrated and the useful bits stay.
I'd tell friends we still have to **learn properly**.
think: I'd be **calm**, since my degree stays valuable and the family firm goes on.
I can see a **future**: graduate, work, then maybe start something.
do: Keep the **weekend shifts** at the showroom.
Build a small **lighting controller** for the shop.
Apply for a summer job at an **electronics firm**.
S0.quote: I can spend the next few years building a skill without worrying that the ground will move.
fieldNote: Bilal's calm is based on a **visible path** and a family firm that has survived bad winters.
He uses AI to understand, then **rebuilds the circuit himself** to check.
He sees the building trade's cycles as normal, not as a crisis.

steps.text: Keep working weekends at the family showroom
Build a lighting controller for the showroom

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like any change in business: some people will win and some will lose, and the winners are the ones who adapt. I'd say that the government shouldn't hand out money, but should make it easy for people to retrain and start things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry a bit for the paperwork side of the family firm. Mum does the invoices on a computer, and a program could do that. But the tiling itself, with a person kneeling on a floor, that's fine for a good while. For my own work, electronics is half thinking and half hands-on, so I'd be partly protected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools more, to get ahead of the other first-years. I'd choose modules on embedded systems and power electronics, where you handle real equipment. And I'd start learning how to run a small business, because the people who own the tools do better than those who just use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a manageable way. It's the sense of a wave coming, and I'd want to be on a board, not under it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd show your dad how AI saves time. What would you show him first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The family firm could use AI in ordering and quoting. I'd show Dad, because he's stubborn about change, but he listens to results. If I can show that it saves him an hour a day, he'll agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by waiting for something to be proven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my advantage is that I'm patient. A lot of people rush at the new thing, but I wait for it to be proven, and then I move fast. That worked when I switched to using AI for explanations. I tried it for a month before I trusted it.

say: I'd say **winners adapt**, and the government should make retraining and starting up easy.
I'd say it **shouldn't hand out money**.
think: Mum's **invoice work** at the family firm could go to a program.
Electronics is half thinking and half **hands-on**, so I'm partly protected.
do: Use the tools more to **get ahead** of other first-years.
Choose **embedded systems** and power electronics modules.
Learn how to **run a small business**.
feel: **Uneasy** but manageable, like wanting to be on the board, not under the wave.
S1.quote: A lot of people rush at the new thing, but I wait for it to be proven, and then I move fast.
fieldNote: Bilal's approach is **patient adoption**: test for a month, then move quickly.
He wants to **own** tools, not only use them, which fits his free-market leaning.
He sees a small gain for the family firm in ordering and quoting.

steps.text: Use an AI tutor for circuit analysis every week
Take embedded systems and power electronics modules
Show Dad an AI quoting tool for the showroom
Read a small business book each term

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, this is too quick for anyone to cope. I wouldn't be political about it, I'd say plainly that families will be left with bills and no plan. I'd say we should look out for each other first, in the family and the community.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be anxious. If the thinking work goes in two years, then the electronics design jobs I'm training for would go early. And the showroom would feel it, because if people lose jobs, they stop renovating their houses. Dad's income could drop sharply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Dad about the firm's savings and how long it could hold on. I'd stop spending on anything that isn't needed. And I'd look at the hands-on side of electronics, like installing and repairing equipment, which would stay for a while after the thinking part is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's a tight feeling in my chest, and I'd try to calm it with prayer and by talking to my older cousin, who runs a repair business. He's been through a recession.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people stop renovating when they lose jobs. How would the showroom cope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mosque community would matter. People there help each other with work leads and small loans, and I'd expect that to be even more important. I'd also offer my help to others, since I can fix things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the mosque community matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my younger sister, Samira, who's fifteen, not to be afraid, and that we'll manage as a family. I wouldn't promise anything, but I'd promise that we won't be alone.

say: I'd say it's **too quick** for anyone to cope.
I'd say we should **look out** for each other first, in family and community.
think: The **electronics design** jobs I'm training for could go early.
If people lose jobs they stop renovating, and **Dad's income** could drop sharply.
do: Talk to Dad about the firm's **savings** and how long it could last.
Look at **hands-on electronics**, like installing and repairing equipment.
feel: **Anxious**, a tight chest, which prayer and talking to my cousin would ease.
S2.quote: If people lose jobs, they stop renovating their houses.
fieldNote: Bilal links the AI shock to the **housing and renovation market**, a clear chain for a tile business.
His response is community-based: **mosque and family**, plus a cousin who survived a recession.
He promises his sister Samira that the family will not be alone, not that all will be fine.

steps.text: Ask Dad how many months the firm could last
Stop buying anything that is not needed
Ask my cousin about repair and installation work
Use the mosque's job leads and small loans if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready, and the best thing is to build real skills and some savings. I'd say it to friends and at the mosque, and I'd keep it practical. I'd say don't panic, but don't ignore it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine in the first part, and I'd worry about the second. I'd have around two years of work in electronics before the thinking part really bites. Then it's about staying useful, and maybe running my own small firm doing installation and repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, take a job in an electronics firm, and save hard. I'd learn the practical, hands-on side. Maybe I'd go into business with my cousin. And I'd put a bit into index funds, because owning a share of the machines is better than competing with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I wouldn't call it fear. It's more like a long exam: you know it's coming, and you prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might go into business with your cousin. What kind of business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad's firm would need to adapt as well. Five years is enough to start using AI for quotes and ordering, and to train his fitters in things that last, like heating and wiring. I'd help him plan that, since I'll be at home in the holidays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you help your dad plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the best protection is having something real to offer. A person who can fix, install and advise is hard to replace. That's the approach I'd take.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** to build real skills and savings.
I'd say **don't panic**, but don't ignore it.
think: I'd be fine at first and worry about the **second part**.
I'd have around **two years** of electronics work before it bites.
do: Finish the degree, take an **electronics job** and save hard.
Learn the **hands-on side**, maybe go into business with my cousin.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a long exam you know is coming.
S3.quote: Owning a share of the machines is better than competing with them.
fieldNote: Bilal's plan is **ownership**: a share in the machines and a small firm of his own.
He treats the future as a long exam, a calm, **prepare and wait** attitude.
He wants to help his dad's firm train fitters in things that last.

steps.text: Take a graduate job at an electronics firm
Save a third of my pay each month
Buy index funds with a small monthly amount
Plan an installation and repair business with my cousin

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and what matters is how people use it. I'd say that work and apprenticeships will keep their value, and that people should avoid waiting for help and start getting ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be calm. Ten years is long enough for me to graduate, work, save, and maybe start something. I'd be 28, with experience and perhaps a family. I'd worry about the world, but not about whether I could cope myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and work for a few years. I'd learn the business side, and maybe take over part of Dad's firm, or start my own electronics service. I'd also marry, if it's meant to be, and I'd want to be settled by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of curiosity. If everything goes the way I plan, I'd be proud of the choices I've made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a family firm has strength. What does trust do for a business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring my cousin, my dad and maybe a couple of friends into one business. There's strength in family firms, because people trust each other. I think that kind of trust is worth a lot when everything else changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the part you can't control?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The only real unknown is how the world handles it. I can control my part, but I can't control the government. I'd vote, volunteer, and help where I can, but I'd focus on being useful.

say: I'd say ten years is **a gift** and depends on how it's used.
I'd say **apprenticeships** will keep their value.
think: I'd be **calm**: ten years is long enough to graduate, work, save and start something.
I'd worry about **the world**, not whether I could cope.
do: Finish the degree and work a few **years**.
Learn the **business side** and maybe start my own electronics service.
**Vote and volunteer**, but focus on being useful.
S4.quote: There's strength in family firms, because people trust each other.
fieldNote: Bilal values **trust and family firms**, which fits his traditional outlook.
He separates what he can control from what he can't, a **practical, steady** habit.
His plans include marriage and settling down, with work as part of a wider life.

steps.text: Finish the degree and work a few years
Save for a deposit and start-up costs
Start an electronics service with my cousin
Vote in every election and volunteer locally

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one. Two years doesn't give my family's firm time to adjust, and it doesn't give me time to build skills. What would help is a plan to help small businesses change, simple loans for retraining, and honest information from the people in charge.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that my generation isn't as anxious about new things as people say. We want to work and look after our families. We just want a fair chance to do it, and we'll do the rest.

headlineQuote: My generation isn't as anxious about new things as people say. We want to work and look after our families.
portrait: Bilal is an **18-year-old** electronic engineering student who works weekends in his family's tile showroom.
He is traditional, **steady** and patient, testing new tools for a month before trusting them.
His faith and **community** at the mosque are his support, with family and a cousin close by.
His moods rise to anxious when the family firm's income is at risk, and stay **calm** with ten years.
He plans for **ownership**, with index funds and an installation and repair business.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario worries him most, since the family firm and his own skills would have no time.
whatWouldHelp: A plan for **small businesses**, simple retraining loans and honest information from leaders.
